      STATEN CREEK RANCH’S EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

I.         INTRODUCTION
           Staten Realty, LLC (“Staten Creek Ranch,” Party #390) respectfully submits these

Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) issued in this proceeding on August 20, 2026.

Staten Creek Ranch supports the PFD’s recommendation that the Commission deny this CCN

application for the reasons discussed therein. 1 However, if the Commission grants this CCN, it

should not adopt the PFD’s recommendation of Route 894 (a Central Corridor route) and should

instead adopt a Northern Corridor route—specifically, Route 392 or Route 410—or, alternatively,

a Southern Corridor route such as Route 296.


           As discussed in Staten Creek Ranch’s prior briefing, the routes that received significant

support in this proceeding can be grouped into three “corridors” based on where they cross the

Colorado River:




1
    See PFD at 148-149.

                                                   1
        •   The “Northern Corridor” routes (Routes 392 and 410) cross the Colorado River

           while paralleling an existing high-voltage transmission line along Segment U3.

       •   The “Central Corridor” routes (Routes 487, 891, and 894) cross the Colorado River

           in close proximity to Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks along either

           Segment J11 or Segment J22.

       •   The “Southern Corridor” routes (Routes 296, 572, and “Cherokee Creek G”) cross

           the Colorado River close to an existing pipeline ROW along Segment J31.

       Staten Creek Ranch strongly supports the selection of Routes 392 and 410, both of which

follow a “Northern Corridor” that would avoid running this line well within a mile of Colorado

Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks, cross the Colorado River while paralleling an existing

transmission line, and take a superior path across open, developed land in the north end of

McCulloch County rather than clearing a new 200-foot right-of-way (ROW) through undeveloped,

densely wooded ranchlands like Staten Creek Ranch.

       The PFD recommends that the Commission select Route 894 if the Commission grants this

CCN. However, a comprehensive evaluation reveals that the Northern Corridor routes travel

through an area that is much more compatible for transmission infrastructure, and would only

marginally increase the cost of this line and its impact on habitable structures. As detailed below,

this is a case where the Commission should place substantial weight on the qualitative impacts

that this proposed transmission line would have on the unspoiled natural beauty of two of Texas’s

premier state parks rather than focusing myopically on the incrementally better quantitative

performance of routes along the Central Corridor. While the PFD correctly acknowledges many

of the qualitative impacts that the Central Corridor routes would have on state parks and

undeveloped ranchlands, it does not give those impacts sufficient weight in its routing

                                                 2
 recommendation. Moreover, the PFD’s analysis contains several errors that, if corrected, further

support selecting a Northern Corridor route. As detailed in these Exceptions, the PFD: (1) does

not adequately weigh the impacts of Route 894 on Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks;

(2) does not adequately consider Route 410 as a viable Northern Corridor alternative that addresses

the habitable-structure concerns raised about Route 392; (3) treats paralleling property boundaries

as equivalent to paralleling existing compatible infrastructure, overstating Route 894’s

performance on that criterion; and (4) understates the qualitative harms that the Central Corridor

would inflict on undeveloped ranchlands in McCulloch County.

       Finally, while Staten Creek Ranch does not believe that the Southern Corridor routes

perform as well as those in the Northern Corridor, Staten Creek is unopposed to those routes, as

they would at least mitigate the extreme qualitative downsides of the Central Corridor routes while

performing similarly on a quantitative basis.

               894 would have on Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks.
       The Commission is statutorily required to consider impacts to “recreational and park areas”

when routing transmission lines. 2         That factor should receive substantial weight in the

Commission’s analysis because all routes that use the Central Corridor, 3 including the PFD’s

proposed Route 894, would severely impact both Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks.

Collectively, Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks cover approximately 8,500 acres on

either side of a section of the Colorado River. 4 Colorado Bend State Park attracts tens of thousands

Rock and Colorado Bend State Parks and sought to protect from the impacts of a transmission line

impact the experience of park visitors. 40 Texas state parks are an invaluable public resource, and

developed landscapes and experience unspoiled natural beauty.                     In prior CCN cases, the

parks. And importantly, Commission precedent illustrates that there is nothing magical about the

½ mile “visual foreground” metric shown in the EA tables, which the PFD relies on heavily.
